Notifications and VPN consent are separate checks before a connection can start.

The simulated connection is ready. HTTPS trust and successful capture still need independent verification.

A real desktop will approve or reject this phone. No enrollment request is sent yet; choose an outcome to explore the next state.
Paste the pairing payload from your desktop. Review its identity before continuing. QR scanning is not available in this preview.
This payload is a temporary credential. It is hidden here, kept out of diagnostics, and discarded after review.
Compare the computer name and identity fingerprint with the desktop you intend to use. A route address is not proof of identity.
Active capture will need a visible notification with a Stop action. This preview simulates the permission choice without requesting an Android permission.
Android allows one VPN per user or profile. Starting capture can replace another VPN. This choice only advances the preview; no Android VPN is started.
Another VPN is marked active in this scenario. A real connection would need your explicit Android consent to replace it.
Choose installed apps or explore the sample list. Selection does not start capture.
Example apps keep the preview separate from your installed-app list.

An app you control can explicitly trust a development CA.

Connect with a clear trust boundary
Pairing, VPN permission, HTTPS trust, and successful traffic are different checks. This preview helps you explore them separately.

Start pairing from the desktop, paste its invitation, and compare the displayed identity before continuing. The desktop must approve each phone. A familiar display name alone is not proof of identity.
2. Select apps and allow VPN access
The finished app will request Android VPN consent and show an ongoing Stop notification. Only selected apps belong in the capture interface. Starting a VPN can replace another active VPN.
Pairing, VPN consent and an installed CA do not verify HTTPS interception. Prepare trust for an app you control, then verify a real test request separately.
Preparation only · HTTPS and traffic are not verified. This preview does not download, install or check a certificate.
The gateway certificate identifies the computer and encrypts the phone connection. The interception CA signs certificates for captured sites. A gateway pin is not the interception CA fingerprint.

Obtain only the public interception CA certificate from the computer you trust. Compare the SHA-256 fingerprint of that exact certificate with the fingerprint displayed by the trusted computer. Stop if they differ. CA and gateway private keys stay on the computer.

In Android Settings, look under Security for Encryption & credentials, Install from storage, or Install a certificate → CA certificate. Names vary by device. Choose the verified public CA file and review Android’s trust warning. On Android 11 and later, CA installation must be done through Settings. Opening Settings or returning here does not confirm installation.
Security settings could not be opened. Open Android Settings manually and look for certificate installation or trusted user credentials.

Installing a user CA does not make every app trust it. For an app you own, the example below bundles one specific public CA only in its debug build, without requiring user-CA installation. It does not change this companion or other apps.

This complete example is for an app with no existing Network Security Configuration. If yours has one, keep its manifest reference, domains, trust anchors and pin sets. Merge only the debug-overrides block into a debug variant of that configuration; keep the release configuration unchanged.
Place the verified public CA certificate here in PEM or DER form. Include no private key. These files belong to your own app’s debug source set.
Copy is unavailable. Select the example text to copy it manually.

The explicit overridePins=false keeps Android Network Security Configuration pin checks enforced. Libraries can use their own certificate pins or trust settings and still reject interception. This example does not bypass those checks or guarantee HTTPS capture.

In Android Settings, find trusted credentials or user certificates and remove this CA when it is no longer needed. Remove the added public CA and debug-only configuration from your own app, preserving any settings it already had. Forgetting a computer in the companion does not uninstall Android user CAs.

The planned preview intercepts selected HTTP and HTTPS over TCP ports 80 and 443. DNS stays on the underlying phone network. UDP/443 will be blocked to encourage TCP fallback; some apps may fail instead. This is an HTTP debugging tool, not a general privacy VPN.

Stop will close capture and restore normal networking. Forget removes the saved computer credentials; remove a user-installed CA separately in Android settings. Desktop revocation must disconnect that phone. No real network or credentials are changed by this local preview.
Explore safe failure states. These controls only affect the local preview, and recent events never include pairing payloads or traffic.
Use these controls to test recovery and permission flows while the desktop connection is under development.
